passages.happening:
When Nahash king of the Ammonites dies, David says, “I will show kindness to Hanun son of Nahash, because his father showed kindness to me” (verse 2), and sends messengers to console him. But the Ammonite princes say to Hanun, “Have not his servants come to you to explore the land, spy it out, and overthrow it?” (verse 3).

‘So Hanun took David’s servants, shaved their beards, cut off their garments at the hips, and sent them away’ (verse 4). David sends to meet the humiliated men and tells them, “Stay in Jericho until your beards have grown back, and then return” (verse 5).
passages.hearers:
Chapter 18 summed up David's victories in broad strokes. This chapter slows down to tell one campaign, explaining how the war with Ammon began. It follows 2 Samuel 10.

Ammon was a small kingdom east of the Jordan, centered on Rabbah, on the site of modern Amman in Jordan. Its king Nahash had once besieged Jabesh-gilead and been defeated by Saul. The Bible does not say what kindness Nahash showed David. Many suggest he helped David while Saul was pursuing him, since Nahash was Saul's enemy, but the text is silent.

Sending envoys to console a new king on his father's death was standard diplomacy, a way of reaffirming a treaty with the next ruler. The word for kindness, chesed, is the loyal love the last two chapters used of God; between kings it means loyalty within an alliance. Hanun's officials read the visit as spying, a real danger, since envoys could scout a city's defenses. The insult was severe. A full beard marked a man's honor, and shaving it by force was deep disgrace; cutting the garments exposed the men, a shame associated with prisoners. David's word to wait in Jericho spared them further public shame.
passages.later: First Samuel tells how ‘Nahash the Ammonite came up and laid siege to Jabesh-gilead’ (1 Samuel 11:1). Paul wrote, ‘If it is possible on your part, live at peace with everyone’ (Romans 12:18).
passages.asks: David's kindness was read as a trick. Ask whether you have assumed the worst of someone who meant you well. And ask how you protect the dignity of people who have been shamed on your behalf, as David did for his men.

passages.happening:
‘When the Ammonites realized that they had become a stench to David’ (verse 6), they hire chariots and horsemen from the Aramean kingdoms with a thousand talents of silver. David sends Joab and the army (verse 8). Joab finds battle lines before him and behind him, takes the best men against the Arameans, and gives the rest to his brother Abishai against the Ammonites (verses 10-11). He tells Abishai that whichever of them is hard pressed, the other will come to the rescue (verse 12), and then says, “Be strong and let us fight bravely for our people and for the cities of our God. May the LORD do what is good in His sight” (verse 13). The Arameans flee, and so do the Ammonites (verses 14-15).

The Arameans bring more troops from beyond the Euphrates. David gathers all Israel, crosses the Jordan and defeats them (verses 16-18). ‘When Hadadezer’s subjects saw that they had been defeated by Israel, they made peace with David and became subject to him. So the Arameans were unwilling to help the Ammonites anymore’ (verse 19).
passages.hearers:
To become a stench was an idiom for having made oneself odious and provoked hostility. Hiring foreign chariots with silver shows how the smaller states of the region bought military power. A talent was the largest unit of weight, commonly estimated at around thirty kilograms.

At the center of the chapter stands Joab's short speech: a call to help one another, to be strong, chazaq, and then to leave the outcome to God. The same call to strength comes back when David charges Solomon (22:13). The chapter ends by reversing its beginning: the Ammonites hired the Arameans to help them, and by the end the Arameans would not help them anymore.

The numbers differ from 2 Samuel 10. There the hired troops total thirty-three thousand men; here verse 7 speaks of thirty-two thousand chariots. Verse 18 has seven thousand charioteers, where 2 Samuel 10:18 has seven hundred. Copying errors in numbers were common in ancient manuscripts, and scholars also note that the Hebrew word often translated thousand can sometimes mean a military unit. In Samuel this war frames the story of David and Bathsheba, told during the siege of Rabbah (2 Samuel 11-12). The Chronicler passes over that story and keeps his eye on the kingdom and the temple to come.
passages.later: Second Samuel tells the same end of the battle: ‘David killed seven hundred charioteers and forty thousand foot soldiers’ (2 Samuel 10:18). Paul gave a similar charge: ‘Be on the alert. Stand firm in the faith. Be men of courage. Be strong’ (1 Corinthians 16:13).
passages.asks: Joab made his plan, promised to come to his brother's rescue, and then left the outcome with God. Ask who you have promised to stand with if things go badly. And ask whether you can do your part fully and still pray, ‘May the LORD do what is good in His sight’ (verse 13).
